extracted.intended_audience: readers of Popular Science Monthly — scientifically interested general public, students and instructors in physics/chemistry
extracted.subtask_description: Practical description and demonstration of liquefying 'permanent' gases (Cailletet/Pictet methods), including apparatus design, experimental procedure, observational signs, and safety/educational considerations. Also discusses basic probability rules relevant to scientific reasoning and demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication rule for conditional probabilities (chain rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The probability that C follows from A may be obtained by multiplying the probability that B follows from A by the probability that C follows from B — when the classes of propositions are so selected that the probability of C following from any B in general is the same as the probability of C following from the B which is deducible from A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This holds under restrictions (classes selected so probabilities match) which are often of little consequence in practice; the text notes this is 'usually recognized as a principle universally true' but that care about the selection of proposition classes is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of approximate independence (supplementary rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a frequently used supplementary rule that when the probability that C is true if B is substantially the same as the probability that C is true if A, one may treat them as equal for calculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule 'is not universally valid' and requires 'greatest caution' — double care: (1) never use it when it will involve serious error; (2) never fail to take advantage of it when it can be employed. Examples: assuming the proportion of male births is the same in all months; card-shuffling approximations where imperfect shuffling can produce measurable departures (empirical count example: expected 85 vs observed 94 hands with 3 or 4 spades in 165 hands).

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence considerations and cautions in applied probability
rubrics_metrics.description: In practical applications the question whether two events may be considered independent is often 'an exceedingly nice question' — independence (probability under B equals probability under A) is easy in games of chance but delicate in ordinary life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize approximations (e.g., assuming thorough shuffling) can be false in practice; empirical checks (counts, repeat trials) are useful to detect departures from assumed independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sign of liquefaction on sudden pressure release
rubrics_metrics.description: On suddenly releasing compressed gas there appears 'a dense mist' or 'a heavy mist' in the capillary glass tube; this mist is 'an infallible sign of the liquefaction, or even the congelation, of the gases.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mist is formed under influence of external cold produced by sudden removal of pressure (Poisson cooling); observation of mist/droplets (including 'pulverized liquid' forming then consolidating to a column) is used as evidence for liquefaction — duration and appearance (e.g., persists more than three seconds) are noted as part of confirming signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thermodynamic/critical-point requirement for liquefaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Permanent gases require a certain combination of pressure and reduced temperature (a critical point): either compression or refrigeration alone, however intense, may be insufficient; both must meet the gas-specific critical conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: bioxide of nitrogen remained gaseous at 270 atmospheres and +8°C; formene liquefies at 180 atmospheres and +1°C; oxygen and carbonic oxide at −29°C and ~300 atm still gaseous until sudden release; hydrogen required ~280 atmospheres and specific procedures to observe liquefaction. Use Poisson's formula to estimate cooling on expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparatus design criteria for gas-liquefaction experiments (Cailletet system)
rubrics_metrics.description: The apparatus consists of a strong steel cylinder with a plunger-piston, leather packing, a steel reservoir capable of ~900–1000 atmospheres, metallic capillary tubes connecting components, a glass capillary tube to hold the gas, concentric glass cylinders for freezing mixtures, and manometers (modified Thomasset and glass manometer) for verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design features: reservoir connected to mercury which compresses the gas; capillary gas tube can be surrounded by freezing mixtures or liquid protoxide of nitrogen; outer cylinder contains desiccants to prevent ice/vapor deposit; valves/screws to suddenly release compressed gases; manometers should be verified against open manometer readings (field verification). The apparatus should permit spectroscopic or projection examination (adjustable reservoir position).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample preparation requirement: drying and CO2 removal
rubrics_metrics.description: Before attempting to liquefy atmospheric air, the sample 'had been first dried and deprived of every trace of carbonic acid.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper drying and removal of CO2 (and likely other contaminants) is required to avoid false observations or interference with liquefaction behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental loading and compression procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure to prepare the glass tube: pass a current of the gas through the tube to expel atmospheric air, place tube horizontally to fill, close its extremity at a lamp, close the other extremity by the finger and introduce vertically into the iron apparatus dipping into mercury; surround upper part with freezing mixture and cover with bell-glass; connect to compression pump and manometer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compression of water acts on surface of mercury forcing it into the tube and compressing the gas into small drops which unite to form liquid. Use a manometer to show degree of pressure; nuts/screws are used to adjust apparatus and stop passages when pouring mercury. The enlarged lower end of the tube is balanced so it cannot break; ensure upper portion walls are sufficiently strong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation, reproducibility, and witness verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental observations should be repeatable and witnessed; experiments were repeated 'again and again' in the presence of multiple scientists to remove doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document the appearance sequence (fine mist → droplets → column → disappearance), note durations (phenomenon persisting >3 seconds), repeat experiments under controlled conditions, and, where possible, perform demonstrations in presence of other experts to corroborate results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety and handling precautions for high-pressure glass apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: The notable apparatus 'involves no danger' because the glass tube has a very small surface area; the enlarged lower end is subject to equal pressure inside and outside and cannot break; only the upper portion must withstand internal pressure and has very strong walls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design to minimize breakage risk (small glass surface, balanced pressure regions); use strong materials for portions under tension; provide packing to prevent liquid escape; handle mercury and high pressures with appropriate care; choose configurations that limit danger in demonstration settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design criteria for instructional demonstration apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: A small lecture-room or laboratory apparatus (Ducretet copy) should be simple, safe, and allow naked-eye observation of all phases of liquefaction and projection on a screen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include portable pump with manometer, freezing mixture surrounds, bell-glass cover, and projection capability (Drummond light). The instrument should 'render great service in research and in instruction, whether in colleges or in the lecture-room.' Emphasize simplicity and safety to enable routine teaching demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical verification of assumptions about physical media (telephone example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of devices like the telephone demonstrates that 'inert, dead matter' (metal diaphragms) can respond to minute air-particle motions and even surpass biological tympanum in sensitivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret demonstrations (telephone diaphragm transmitting voice with great accuracy) as evidence about physical medium behavior; such demonstrations can inform conceptual arguments (e.g., against treating matter as 'dead') and are useful pedagogically to illustrate physical principles of sound transmission.
